{{Short description|Paradoxical Philosophy}}
'''Mandeville's paradox''' is named after [[Bernard Mandeville]] (1670–1733), who posits that actions which may be qualified as vicious with regard to individuals have benefits for society as a whole. This is alluded to in the subtitle of his most famous work, ''[[The Fable of The Bees: or, Private Vices, Public Benefits]]''. He states that "Fraud, Luxury, and Pride must live; Whilst we the Benefits receive."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Mandeville|first=Bernard|title=[[The Fable of the Bees]]|year=1714|at=‘The Moral’|author-link=Bernard Mandeville}}</ref>

The [[philosophy|philosopher]] and [[economist]] [[Adam Smith]] opposes this (although he defends a moderated version of this line of thought in his theory of the [[invisible hand]]), since Mandeville fails, in his opinion, to distinguish between vice and virtue.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Smith|first=Adam|title=[[The Theory of Moral Sentiments]]|year=1759|at=Part VII, Section II, Chapter 4 (‘Of licentious systems’)|author-link=Adam Smith}}</ref>
